newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico election unnerves Mexicans, but not Wall St.
newsitem.headline: Mexico election unnerves Mexicans, but not Wall St.

text.p: Nervous Mexican investors have been pulling their money out of the country's financial markets ahead of July 6 national elections, during which the ruling party may face its worst defeat ever, analysts say.
But up on Wall Street, the view has been different: the elections may bring short-term uncertainty, but Mexico's economy is on the mend from the 1994-5 crisis and Latin America is hot.
"There is a dichotomy right now between what the local investors and the foreigners are doing," Ed Cabrera, director of Latin American equity strategy at Merrill Lynch in New York, told Reuters.
"The local investor has walked away from the market, but the foreigners see a Latin America-wide rally, cheap prices in Mexico and an economy getting stronger, so they say, 'Let's go for it.'"
Despite the notable absence of locals, foreign investors have pushed up stock prices about 13 percent so far in June. On Friday, the bourse closed at a record 4,481 points.

Much of the excitement has been over the economy. Recent data on industrial production and retail sales show an economy on the mend from the 1994-5 crisis and a recovery not only on economists' models but in consumers' pocketbooks.
"The market is much more focused on the economy than politics at the moment, and they like what they see," said Damian Fraser, head of Caspian Research in Mexico City.

If second quarter earnings reports due a week after the poll confirm the recovery has finally boosted company profits, the market could be poised for take-off despite uncertainty from the elections, Cabrera said.

What worries some market watchers, however, is that Wall Street may have missed the significance of the July 6 poll, when Mexicans elect a new lower house in Congress, six state governors and, for the first time, Mexico City's mayor.
Polls released last week showed the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI), in power since 1929, would likely lose its lower house majority for the first time ever.
They also showed leftist veteran Cuauhtemoc Cardenas rolling to victory in the key Mexico City race, which will thrust him into the national spotlight.

Cardenas' victory has been widely predicted, but the specter of a PRI loss in Congress would be more surprising. An opposition victory would usher Mexico's political system, dominated by one party for nearly 70 years, into uncharted territory.

While most analysts say the move would be a long-term plus for Mexico, it could mean President Ernesto Zedillo will have a tougher time passing economic legislation in the lower house, which has power over the budget.
Traditionally, the PRI-dominated Congress has rubber-stamped the budget and most other proposed legislation.

"The (market) always says it has discounted it, but my experience is that when the market sees the news they will react more negatively afterwards," Susan Gilbertson, director of Latin American equity strategy at Paribas in New York, told Reuters.
Fraser and Cabrera agreed that one element the markets have not yet discounted is what happens to the PRI, one of the world's most successful parties, if it suffers an historic defeat.
"The key issue is not whether Zedillo will be able to pass legislation, but how the PRI, and the dinosaurs within the party, are going to react," Cabrera said, referring to the party's old guard.
"Some worry the PRI will swing to the left to react to Cardenas....Some shifting of ground is likely and it will probably be to the left," added Caspian's Fraser.
